findings.requirement_type: Cyber Liability — No Policy Verified in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: Cyber, Network Security and Privacy Liability Insurance with a limit of not less than $5,000,000 per occurrence. The policy shall include ... data breaches ... invasion of privacy ... breach notification costs, credit remediation ... regulatory defense costs plus fines and penalties, cyber extortion, electronic data restoration ... network business interruption, computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity ...
findings.policy_quote: GL: 'This insurance does not apply to ... "bodily injury," "property damage," or "personal and advertising injury" arising directly or indirectly out of any "cyber incident".' (CG 40 35 12 23, Pg 68). Umbrella: 'This insurance does not apply to any liability ... arising out of any "Cyber Incident" ...' (475-0661 01 25, Pg 76). Umbrella also: '... Access or Disclosure of Confidential or Personal Material or Information ...' (475-0654, Pg 72) and '... Violation of Law Addressing Data Privacy ...' (475-0655, Pg 74).
findings.policy_page: Arch GL Pg 56, 64, 68; Hanover Umbrella Pg 72, 74, 76
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires a $5M Cyber policy with extraordinarily broad mandatory components (regulatory fines AND penalties, third-party fidelity, computer fraud, funds transfer, business interruption, cyber extortion, breach notification, etc.). The audit set contains NO standalone cyber policy. The GL absolutely excludes cyber, data breach, and data-privacy violations on three independent endorsements (CG 00 69, CG 21 06, CG 40 35). The Umbrella is identically barred (475-0654, 475-0655, 475-0661). Run-Test handles voter PII for 90M+ registered voters across 31 states + DC — this is one of the most concentrated data-privacy risks possible.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa contractually requires you to carry $5 million of cyber insurance with breach notification, ransomware, business-interruption, regulatory fines, and computer-fraud coverage all in one. Neither of the policies we audited covers ANY of that — the GL excludes it three different ways, and the umbrella excludes it three different ways. If a standalone cyber policy isn't already in your program, this is the single biggest exposure in your entire risk portfolio: a ransomware event or voter-data breach during election season would be uninsured AND would put you in immediate breach of the Maricopa contract.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: Confirm whether a standalone Cyber policy is in force for Run-Test. If yes, produce the policy for full audit against §8.2.13's enumerated requirements (regulatory fines AND penalties is a sticking point on most forms — verify the carrier provides true affirmative coverage, not just defense). If no, bind a $5M cyber tower (likely primary $3M-$5M plus excess) immediately — this is a contractual material breach trigger and a balance-sheet event waiting to happen. Election-vendor cyber programs typically need: voter-PII coverage, dependent business interruption (counties as dependent customers), social engineering, and regulatory coverage including state secretary-of-state investigations.
discoveryQuestions: You handle voter data for over 90 million Americans across 31 states — when was the last time you sat with your cyber broker and walked through what happens, hour by hour, after a ransomware event the week before an election?
Maricopa requires regulatory fines AND penalties coverage, not just defense. Most cyber forms exclude or sublimit fines — do you know what your current cyber form actually pays for?
If the Maricopa County recorder served you with a contract default notice tomorrow because they couldn't see proof of $5M cyber, what would you put in front of them in the next 24 hours?
Have you tested your incident response plan against the timing of an election? A 14-day notification window during early voting is a different conversation than the same window in March.

findings.requirement_type: Professional Liability / Tech E&O — No Policy Verified in Audit Set
findings.contract_quote: PROFESSIONAL LIABILITY OR ERRORS AND OMISSIONS LIABILITY: $1,000,000 per claim and aggregate. ... UMBRELLA or Excess Liability ... shall provide liability coverages that at least follow form over the underlying insurance requirements ... for Commercial General Liability, Commercial Automobile Liability, Employers' Liability, and any other liability coverage (other than Professional Liability) ...
findings.policy_quote: Hanover Umbrella: 'This insurance does not apply to any liability arising out of the rendering of or failure to render any professional services, advice, or instruction ...' (475-0031 12 14, Pg 46). Arch GL Coverage D E&O Extension: 'subject to General Aggregate AND Each Occurrence limits — shared with A/B/C, NOT a separate aggregate' (00 GL1049 00 01 25, Pg 23).
findings.policy_page: Hanover Umbrella Pg 46; Arch GL Pg 23
findings.gap_description: Sacramento requires $1M per claim/aggregate Professional Liability and expressly forbids using the umbrella to satisfy this minimum. The audit set contains no standalone Professional Liability/Tech E&O policy. The Arch GL provides a heavily limited E&O extension (Coverage D) that shares limits with A/B/C, applies only to the declared SECURITY classifications (98751/91636/91127), and contains numerous exclusions — it does not insure election-services professional exposure. The Umbrella has an absolute Professional Liability exclusion. Run-Test's core operations (ballot printing accuracy, mail-sort error, signature-verification software, election-mail processing) are professional services subject to Tech E&O / Miscellaneous E&O claims.
findings.plain_english: Sacramento County requires $1M of professional liability — separate from your umbrella — to cover errors in your election services. We don't see a standalone E&O policy in this set. The bit of E&O coverage that's bolted onto your security-guards GL (Coverage D) shares its limits with the regular GL and only covers your declared security operations — not ballot processing or election mail. The umbrella's professional services exclusion means a single signature-verification error claim could exhaust your underlying limit with zero excess to fall back on.
findings.recommendation: URGENT: Confirm whether a Tech E&O / Miscellaneous Professional Liability policy is in force. If yes, audit the 'Professional Services' definition word-for-word — it must affirmatively include ballot printing, mail-sort, signature verification, software/hardware solutions, and any SaaS components. Verify retro date on/before earliest Sacramento contract date and on/before 11/01/2021 for Maricopa (per §8.2.3 retro requirement). If no, bind standalone Tech E&O of at least $1M each claim/aggregate immediately. Election-services E&O is a niche market — placement should consider higher than $1M given the per-state regulatory exposure.
discoveryQuestions: If a county discovers 12,000 ballots were misprinted or mis-sorted in your facility two weeks before an election, what does your professional liability policy actually say about ballot printing being a 'professional service'?

When was your retroactive date set, and have you continuously renewed claims-made coverage since then? Sacramento requires retro on or before contract effective date — Maricopa requires retro before 11/01/2021.
Sacramento's contract specifically prohibits using the umbrella to satisfy the $1M E&O minimum. Do you know if your current standalone E&O is exactly $1M, or higher?
Has your E&O carrier seen a copy of your election-services service catalog? You'd be surprised how many forms quietly carve out 'mail-services' or 'data-processing' as non-professional.

findings.contract_quote: [Cyber must include] computer fraud coverage, funds transfer loss, third-party fidelity, theft, no requirement for arrest and conviction ...
findings.policy_quote: Not applicable — no Crime/Fidelity policy in audit set.
findings.gap_description: Maricopa's cyber spec embeds 'third-party fidelity' and 'computer fraud' / 'funds transfer loss' obligations. Audit set contains no Commercial Crime/Fidelity policy. Run-Test as a PE-backed manufacturer and government contractor is a typical buyer of Crime coverage — verify presence and adequacy.
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants you to insure third-party theft, computer fraud, and funds-transfer fraud. Some cyber policies include these; many sublimit them to $250k or less. A standalone Commercial Crime policy is the cleaner answer, especially with PE ownership and government contracting exposure. We don't see one in this audit set — confirm whether one is in force.
findings.recommendation: Confirm whether a Commercial Crime policy is in force (employee theft, third-party crime including client property, computer fraud, funds-transfer fraud, social engineering with full-limit endorsement, client-property coverage). If yes, audit. If no, evaluate placement — PE-backed manufacturer with multi-county government clients is a classic Crime buyer.
discoveryQuestions: Have you ever had an employee theft incident, or a near-miss with a fraudulent vendor invoice or wire transfer request?
Does your CFO know who has dual-control authority on outbound wires, and who would approve a $500k transfer if the CEO's email asked for it?
If Maricopa County's payment processor was compromised and $1M of contract payments were diverted, would your insurance respond to make you whole?

findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance ... shall not contain any provisions which would serve to limit third party action over claims.
findings.policy_quote: 'This insurance applies only to the insured's operations for which a classification is listed on the declaration page of this policy. If any classification is not shown, the corresponding insured's operations is not insured hereunder.' Classifications: 91127 Alarms Install / 91636 Detective or Investigative / 98751 Security and Patrol Agencies. (00 GL0713 00 08 11, Pg 39 + Schedule Pg 38)
findings.gap_description: The Arch GL is a SECURITY-OPERATIONS-ONLY monoline. It applies exclusively to the three declared security classifications (91127, 91636, 98751). It would NOT respond to ballot printing, election mail processing, or any of Run-Test's core election-services operations. If a county COI ever named this policy as the GL response, it would fail the moment a claim came in on non-security operations. This needs explicit operational segregation — and the 'main' GL (Citizens) is the policy that must respond to election services.
findings.plain_english: This policy only covers your in-house security guards — it does not cover ballot printing, mail handling, or election technology work at all. If somebody at the county ever pulled a COI showing this policy and a claim arose from a printing error or ballot-handling incident, there's zero coverage on this policy. Make absolutely sure no COI ever names this policy as your election-services GL response.

(2) Audit Run-Test's COI library to ensure no county has a COI referencing Arch BSPKG0356704 as the GL response. findings.requirement_type: GL — Additional Insured Ongoing & Completed Operations (Arch Security GL)
findings.contract_quote: The COUNTY ... are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects: liability arising out of activities performed by or on behalf of the CONTRACTOR; products and completed operations of the CONTRACTOR ...
findings.policy_quote: CG 20 10 12 19 (Ongoing): 'ALL PARTIES WHERE REQUIRED BY A WRITTEN CONTRACT PROVIDED SUCH CONTRACT WAS EXECUTED PRIOR TO LOSS' (Pg 60). CG 20 37 12 19 (Completed Operations): same blanket schedule (Pg 62).
findings.gap_description: Arch GL has both blanket-by-contract AI endorsements (CG 20 10 ongoing + CG 20 37 completed operations). Together they satisfy Sacramento's ongoing+completed AI requirement. Two technical caveats: (i) 'executed prior to loss' wording (vs more common 'prior to occurrence' or 'prior to work'); (ii) AI 'not broader than required by contract' clause caps to lesser of contract or policy. Useful confirmation but does not change compliance posture.
findings.plain_english: On the security-guards GL, your additional-insured endorsements for both ongoing and completed work are blanket — counties are automatically picked up as additional insureds as long as the contract is signed before the loss. That's the right structure. We still need to verify the same is true on the primary Citizens CGL.
findings.recommendation: Mirror this AI structure on the Citizens primary CGL — confirm CG 20 10 + CG 20 37 (or equivalent later editions) are present with blanket-by-contract schedules. Verify edition dates: 12 19 retains 'caused, in whole or in part by' language but caps AI scope to contract requirement.

findings.requirement_type: GL — 'Arising Out Of' AI Trigger vs CG 20 10 12 19 'Caused In Whole Or In Part'
findings.contract_quote: The COUNTY ... are to be endorsed as additional insureds as respects: liability arising out of activities performed by or on behalf of the CONTRACTOR ... The coverage shall contain no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection afforded to the COUNTY ...
findings.policy_quote: CG 20 10 12 19: 'caused, in whole or in part, by: 1. Your acts or omissions; or 2. The acts or omissions of those acting on your behalf ... However, the insurance afforded to such additional insured: ... Will not be broader than that which you are required by the contract or agreement to provide.' (Pg 60)
findings.gap_description: Sacramento contract uses 'arising out of' (broadest AI trigger). The 12 19 edition CG 20 10 narrows AI to liability 'caused in whole or in part by' the named insured — and further caps coverage to 'not broader than required by contract.' The 'not broader than required' clawback technically restores 'arising out of' if the contract demands it, but underwriters and adjusters often resist. Pre-2013 CG 20 10 (07 04 edition) used 'arising out of' directly. This is also a nominal violation of Sacramento's 'no endorsed limitations on the scope of protection' clause.
findings.plain_english: Your contract demands the broadest 'arising out of' trigger for additional insureds — meaning the county is covered any time a claim has anything to do with your work. The current AI endorsement uses narrower 'caused in whole or in part by' language, with a clause that caps it to whatever the contract requires. In theory that snaps back to the contract's 'arising out of.' In practice, an adjuster looking for a reason to deny will run with the narrower wording. Sacramento's 'no endorsed limitations' clause technically gives them grounds to reject the COI.
findings.recommendation: Confirm same review of Citizens primary CGL AI endorsement. Where possible, request a manuscript AI endorsement using 'arising out of' language. If carrier will not change, document the contract-controls language in writing with carrier so an adjuster cannot rely on the narrower language. Consider CG 20 33 (broader blanket AI) on renewal.
discoveryQuestions: Has any county risk manager ever flagged the 'caused in whole or in part by' language on your AI endorsement?
If a county was sued for something only loosely tied to your work — say, a slip-and-fall on a county-owned sidewalk during ballot delivery — would your AI endorsement defend them?
When your COI is issued, does the certificate language describe AI coverage in 'arising out of' terms or 'caused by' terms?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa GL — $2M Each Occurrence vs Arch $1M
findings.contract_quote: Commercial General Liability (CGL) insurance and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance with a limit of not less than $2,000,000 for each occurrence, $4,000,000 Products/Completed Operations Aggregate, and $4,000,000 General Aggregate Limit.
findings.policy_quote: Arch GL: 'GENERAL AGGREGATE LIMIT $3,000,000; PRODUCTS/COMPLETED OPS AGGREGATE $3,000,000; PERSONAL & ADV INJURY $1,000,000; EACH OCCURRENCE $1,000,000.' Underlying Citizens primary (per Hanover Schedule): '$1,000,000 Each Occurrence / $1,000,000 PI&AI / $2,000,000 General Aggregate.' Hanover Umbrella: $10M each occurrence / $10M Gen Agg / $10M Products-Completed Ops Agg.
findings.policy_page: Arch GL Dec; Hanover Umbrella Pg 14; Hanover Umbrella Dec
findings.gap_description: Maricopa requires $2M each occurrence / $4M Gen Agg / $4M Prod-Comp Ops. Citizens primary CGL is $1M each occurrence / $2M Gen Agg. §8.2.10 expressly permits umbrella stacking ('and, if necessary, Commercial Umbrella insurance'). Hanover Umbrella at $10M follows form over Citizens, so $1M + $10M = $11M each occurrence (>$2M) and aggregates similarly. Compliance achieved via umbrella stack — ARCH security GL is not in this calculation. Per-occurrence/aggregate compliant via stacking; should confirm umbrella follows form on products-completed ops aggregate (Hanover umbrella shows $10M Products-Completed Ops Agg so OK).
findings.plain_english: Maricopa wants $2M each occurrence on GL. Your primary is $1M, but Maricopa's contract specifically allows you to use the umbrella to get there, and you have a $10M umbrella sitting on top. Total tower: $11M. You meet the limit through stacking. We just need to confirm the COI clearly shows the umbrella sitting over the GL.
findings.recommendation: On COIs to Maricopa, ensure the umbrella line clearly references coverage over the underlying CGL (per §8.2.9 — 'Certificate of Insurance shall indicate which lines the Commercial Umbrella Insurance covers'). No coverage gap, but COI accuracy is the compliance risk.
discoveryQuestions: When you issue COIs to Maricopa, does the Umbrella row of the certificate explicitly note that it sits over the GL?
Has Maricopa's risk manager ever asked you to confirm umbrella attachment in writing?

discoveryQuestions: Do your ink suppliers' SDS sheets show any phthalates — DEHP, DINP, BBP, DBP?

findings.requirement_type: Maricopa — Indemnity Not Limited by Insurance Limits

discoveryQuestions: Has your PE sponsor stated minimum insurance limit requirements in the investment documents?
If Maricopa lost an election due to a vendor error tied to Run-Test and a class of 500,000 voters sued, what's the floor on damages exposure?
When did you last benchmark your liability tower against other election-services peers — Tenex, Konnech, Hart, Election Systems & Software?

findings.plain_english: Maricopa technically has the right to make you put up a bond or letter of credit to back your insurance deductibles or self-insured retentions. findings.recommendation: (1) Establish (or audit) Run-Test's internal carrier-notice intake workflow with 2-business-day Maricopa pass-through. (2) Add Designated Entity NOC endorsement (see finding #019). (3) Build a renewal calendar with 60-day pre-renewal flag.

If you have any other liability coverage (foreign liability for international travel, longshore for waterfront, etc.), the umbrella ignores it. Also, any sublimited coverage inside your existing policies is invisible to the umbrella unless separately scheduled.
findings.recommendation: (1) Inventory all liability lines and confirm umbrella schedule completeness. (2) If Foreign Voluntary or USL&H is present (even if just 'if any'), schedule on umbrella. (3) For any meaningful sublimits in underlying policies, evaluate whether to schedule them.

findings.gap_description: Standard-market umbrella with defense outside limits — preferred posture. E&S umbrellas often have defense INSIDE limits, which would erode coverage. This Hanover form is the right structure.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella's defense costs are paid OUTSIDE the policy limits — meaning your $10M limit goes entirely toward indemnity, and legal fees are separate. That's the better structure (E&S umbrellas often have defense inside limits, which can chew up your coverage).
findings.recommendation: Maintain at renewal — confirm no carrier change to inside-limits structure.

findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella Checklist Item 6: Maintenance of underlying insurance. Must the insured notify the carrier of any underlying changes?
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 §VIII Conditions Maintenance of Underlying Insurance (Pg 36): Insured must maintain underlying in full force; reduction/exhaustion does not increase umbrella obligations; if underlying limits are reduced, umbrella applies as if underlying limits were maintained.
findings.gap_description: Standard maintenance-of-underlying provision. If Run-Test reduces a primary limit (e.g., shifts to lower auto from $1M to $500k), the umbrella attaches as if $1M were still in place — meaning Run-Test self-insures the gap. This isn't a defect, but it's a process risk: any change to underlying limits without telling Hanover (or in ignorance of the umbrella scheduling) creates an uninsured gap.
findings.plain_english: If you ever change anything on your primary policies — limits, retentions, additional insureds — without telling Hanover, your umbrella may not respond properly. The umbrella treats your primary as if it's at the limits originally scheduled, even if you've quietly downgraded. Process discipline matters here.
findings.recommendation: (1) Establish broker workflow: any change to underlying limits/coverage triggers an umbrella re-cert + Schedule of Underlying update. (2) Annual pre-renewal review of Schedule of Underlying against actual underlying policies.
discoveryQuestions: Has any underlying policy limit been reduced in the past 12 months — even temporarily?
Who at Run-Test would update the umbrella schedule if a primary policy changed mid-term?

findings.contract_quote: RMF Umbrella Checklist Item 10: Punitive damages, are they excluded?
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 §VII.3.l Coverage B (Pg 35): 'No coverage for punitive, exemplary, multiplied damages, taxes, fines, or penalties.'
findings.gap_description: Coverage B (true umbrella) excludes punitive damages, multipliers, fines, and penalties. Coverage A follows form on what underlying covers — so if Citizens primary CGL covers punitive (depends on state law and form), Coverage A might too; but Coverage B is silent. AZ does not insure punitives by statute. CA permits insurance of punitives but it's policy-specific. Election-services litigation often involves potential punitive exposure (intentional voter suppression theories, civil rights violations), so this gap matters.
findings.plain_english: Your umbrella's true-umbrella layer (Coverage B) excludes punitive damages outright. Election-services lawsuits sometimes seek punitive damages — a $10M underlying verdict could become $30M with punitives, and the umbrella wouldn't respond to the multiplier. State law also limits insurability (Arizona doesn't insure punitives at all). Worth a discussion about offshore wrap-arounds or specific-state policies if punitives become a real exposure profile.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm Citizens primary CGL position on punitives. (2) For high-exposure scenarios (voting rights litigation, civil rights claims), evaluate punitive damage wrap-around (Bermuda or offshore captive structures). (3) Document the exclusion in board reporting on uninsured exposures.
discoveryQuestions: Have any prior election-related lawsuits against Run-Test or peers sought punitive damages?
Does Run-Test's PE sponsor have a wrap-around or captive structure that backstops punitives?

If a class action over a ballot processing error costs $5M, your standalone Tech E&O burns through and the umbrella does nothing. Election-services E&O often needs $5M–$10M standalone; your $1M underlying (assumed) is light, with no umbrella backstop possible.
findings.recommendation: (1) Once standalone Tech E&O is verified, evaluate increasing limits to $5M minimum. (2) Sacramento expressly bars umbrella from satisfying its $1M E&O minimum — current structure aligns. (3) For Maricopa (which doesn't address E&O explicitly), confirm Tech E&O limits are sufficient on their own. (4) Discuss dedicated Excess E&O placement for Run-Test's election-services exposure.
discoveryQuestions: If a class action over election results affecting 250,000 voters arose from a Run-Test mail-sorting error, do you have an honest sense of total cost — defense plus settlement?
Is your standalone Tech E&O at $1M, or higher? Is there any excess E&O above it?
Would your PE sponsor accept $1M of Tech E&O as the entire response to a major election-day claim?

findings.requirement_type: Umbrella — Recording & Distribution / TCPA / CAN-SPAM Exclusion
findings.contract_quote: n/a
findings.policy_quote: 475-0001 §VII.1.h (Pg 31): No umbrella excess for TCPA, CAN-SPAM, FCRA/FACTA, or similar statutory privacy/communication claims.
findings.gap_description: Run-Test's election-mail business has direct TCPA exposure (any voter contact via auto-dial/text), and CAN-SPAM exposure (voter email outreach). $1,500-per-violation TCPA statutory damages can quickly exceed primary GL limits. Umbrella will not respond.
findings.plain_english: If Run-Test (or a county on Run-Test's behalf) ever sends robocalls, auto-texts, or bulk election-related emails, TCPA class actions are routine. $1,500 per violation × millions of voters = potentially huge. Your umbrella excludes all of this. Coverage has to come from cyber or a specialty TCPA policy.
findings.recommendation: (1) Confirm Run-Test's actual voter-outreach footprint: any robocalls, auto-texts, or mass emails? (2) Verify cyber policy affirmatively covers TCPA/CAN-SPAM (many forms exclude or sublimit). (3) For high-volume outreach, evaluate dedicated TCPA insurance.
